sections.history: Thiruvanchikulam stands near Kodungallur on the Malabar coast, the ancient Muziris country, once the seat of the Chera kings. In the Tevaram it is Tiruvanjaikkalam, and it is the only shrine in Kerala counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams. Its hymns are Sundarar's, among the oldest references to the temple. The place is bound to the friendship of two of the sixty-three Nayanmar saints: Sundarar, the wandering poet of Tamil Shaivism, and Cheraman Perumal Nayanar, the Chera king who ruled from this region and is remembered in the Periyapuranam as his closest friend. Tradition dates the temple to the Chera age, around the eighth century, though some local accounts claim far greater antiquity. The shrine was damaged during the Mysorean invasion of Malabar, when its copper roofing and treasures were looted, and it has since been restored in the Kerala manner.
sections.architecture: This is a Kerala temple, and it looks nothing like the towered shrines of the Tamil plain. Steep sloping roofs of copper and tile shelter the sanctum and its surrounding structures, there is no soaring gopuram, and the wooden eaves and timber detail speak of the Malabar climate and craft. In front of the sanctum stands a sixteen-pillared namaskara mandapam, the hall of prostration, with a renovation date of 1801 recorded on it. Mural paintings of mythological scenes adorn the temple. The presiding Mahadeva is worshipped as Uma Maheshwara, the divine couple, and the temple is said to hold some thirty-three sub-shrines, among the largest number in Kerala. A shrine to Sundarar is among them, so that the saint is honoured within the walls of the temple he loved.
sections.legends: The legend of Thiruvanchikulam is the departure of two friends for Kailash. Cheraman Perumal, the Chera king, had long been a devotee of Shiva and a friend of Sundarar, and the two journeyed together to many shrines. When Sundarar's earthly days were done, he came to Thiruvanchikulam to worship, and Shiva sent a white elephant from Kailash to bear him to the heavenly mountain. Cheraman Perumal, unwilling to be parted from his friend, mounted his horse, and is said to have whispered the sacred five-syllable mantra into its ear so that it rose into the sky and followed the elephant. Both are believed to have reached Kailash from this spot, on the day of Aadi Swathi in July or August. An old account adds that Sundarar sang a decad on his way, which was sent back to Thiruvanchikulam at his request.
sections.festivals: The great memory of the temple is Aadi Swathi, in the Tamil month of Aadi (July–August), when the saint's departure is recalled and Sundarar is taken around the temple on a white elephant with Cheraman Perumal beside him on his horse. The annual festival falls in the Malayalam month of Kumbham (February–March) and coincides with Maha Shivaratri, with an elephant race among the celebrations. The Thiruvathira of Dhanu and a Brahmotsavam in Vaikasi are also observed. The Palliyara pooja, offered in the evening to the divine couple, is sought especially by those praying for harmony in marriage and for children. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the Malayalam and Tamil calendars.
sections.experience: Come with the story of the two friends in mind, and the temple speaks for itself. Enter the quiet precincts under their sloping roofs and pause in the namaskara mandapam before the sanctum of Mahadeva as Uma Maheshwara. Look for the shrine of Sundarar, and for the images of both saints, and let the tale of the white elephant and the whispered mantra settle. The murals and the many small shrines reward a slow circumambulation. Keep the manners of a Kerala temple: men traditionally enter bare-chested in a mundu, and the mood is hushed and devotional. The temple lies just outside Kodungallur, so the visit combines naturally with the town's other ancient shrines.

visit.timings: Typically open in the early morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Kerala temple custom applies: men traditionally wear a mundu (dhoti) and go without a shirt inside the sanctum area, and women wear a saree, set-mundu, or salwar kameez with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left outside the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer courtyard but prohibited inside the sanctum and the inner enclosure, in keeping with Kerala temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple is at Kottappuram, a short distance south of Kodungallur town, which lies on the Kochi–Thrissur coastal road in Thrissur district. Distances quoted in sources range from about 2 to 6 km from the town centre, so ask locally. Kodungallur is served by frequent buses, and autorickshaws and taxis run to the temple. Kochi has the nearest international airport, and the railway stations at Thrissur and in the Kochi region are the usual rail gateways.
